label: Darboux-Moser-Weinstein Theory
notes: Open by framing the lecture as a local-normal-form story spanning printed pages 44 through 48. The theme is that symplectic geometry has no local invariants: every symplectic manifold looks like flat standard space near a point, and the engine that proves this is Moser's relative theorem.

label: No Local Invariants
notes: Contrast symplectic and Riemannian worlds. Riemannian curvature is a genuine local invariant that obstructs flattening, but symplectic forms carry no analogue. Stress that this floppiness is exactly why symplectic geometry studies global and semilocal structure rather than pointwise differential invariants.

label: Darboux's Theorem
notes: State Darboux precisely: around any point there are coordinates in which omega becomes the constant standard form. Emphasize that the chart is local and that the conclusion is a symplectomorphism onto an open set of standard space, so no two symplectic manifolds differ locally.

label: Darboux Coordinates
notes: Introduce the canonical position and momentum coordinates. Explain that omega splitting as a sum of dq wedge dp blocks is the precise meaning of the standard form, and that these coordinates are the symplectic counterpart of an orthonormal frame, though far less rigid.

label: The Moser Trick
notes: Lay out Moser's deformation idea. Interpolate linearly between the two forms, demand the path of diffeomorphisms pull each back to the start, and differentiate to get a homological equation. Cartan's magic formula converts that equation into solving for a time-dependent vector field.

label: Moser Relative Theorem
notes: State the relative version: if two symplectic forms agree at a point, they are equivalent near it by a diffeomorphism fixing that point. The key input is the Poincare lemma, which produces a primitive vanishing to the needed order at the anchor point.

label: Proof of Darboux
notes: Assemble Darboux from the pieces. Pick a symplectic basis to standardize the form at the point by linear algebra, then apply the Moser relative theorem to upgrade pointwise agreement to a genuine local chart. The two-step pattern, anchor then deform, recurs throughout.

label: Relative Moser on a Submanifold
notes: Generalize the anchor from a point to a submanifold. If the two forms agree along all of a submanifold X, Moser produces a diffeomorphism fixing X pointwise and matching the forms nearby. The Poincare lemma is replaced by a relative version with parameters along X.

label: Lagrangian Subspaces
notes: Recall the linear model. A Lagrangian subspace is isotropic of half dimension, and a complement to one can be repaired into a Lagrangian complement by symmetrizing the graph matrix. This pointwise algebra is the seed that the submanifold Moser theorem grows into a normal form.

label: Toward Weinstein
notes: Preview the payoff. The relative Moser theorem on a submanifold is the machine behind Weinstein's neighborhood theorems: a tubular neighborhood of a Lagrangian looks like its cotangent bundle. Mention the coisotropic variant, where equal restricted forms and orthogonal containment replace the Lagrangian hypothesis.

label: Summary
notes: Recap the chain from pages 44 to 48: no local invariants, Darboux flattening, the Moser trick, the relative theorem at a point and along a submanifold, and the setup for Weinstein. Leave students with the slogan that symplectic rigidity is global, while local symplectic geometry is uniform and floppy.
